title: Gambling stocks: how to analyze gambling companies
description: Gambling stocks: the license as moat and risk. How to analyze gambling companies — B2C versus B2B, margins, regulation and the mandatory offer.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Gambling stocks are shares in companies that make money on games of chance — online casino, sports betting, poker and bingo — or on technology and services sold to gambling companies. It is among the most regulated industries: in Sweden a license has been required since the re-regulation on 1 January 2019, and licensed companies reported gambling turnover of 6.9 billion kronor in Q2 2026 — up 2.8 percent on the year, says the Swedish Gambling Authority. AK1A's universe holds the sector's heaviest Swedish name, Evolution, and its economics — the license as moat and risk — is this guide's subject. As always here: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are gambling stocks — the business model decides the analysis

The gambling industry is two industries under one label, and the value of every ratio depends on which one you are looking at. **The operators** — B2C — run gambling sites and apps directly against the consumer. Their economics revolve around customer acquisition: marketing, bonuses and affiliate commissions are large cost items; operators differ mainly in what a customer costs against how long they stay and play. **The suppliers** — B2B — sell platforms and content to the operators. Evolution delivers live casino studios and game hosting; Kambi, the B2B example in the course [Gambling — licensing and regulation](/kurser/se-12-spel), delivers odds engines and risk management. B2B companies are measured on technology scalability and customer concentration — losing a large operator shows immediately in revenue, a classic case of [concentration risk](/kurser/rk-09-koncentrationsrisk).

Both groups share one denominator separating them from most sectors: the form of revenue is decided by the regulator. Gambling tax, fees and license terms determine how much of the player's stake even becomes company revenue — which leads to the guide's core.

## The license — moat and expropriation risk at the same time

Sweden re-regulated its gambling market on 1 January 2019: the state monopoly was replaced by a licensing system under the Swedish Gambling Authority, and companies without a license were banned from marketing gambling in Sweden. The license is at once the sector's moat and its biggest risk. A moat, because a permit is an entry barrier: competition is limited to those approved and paying the gambling tax — in Sweden 18 percent of net revenue. A risk, because the same regulator can change the terms: deposit limits, advertising and bonus rules have tightened repeatedly since 2019, each time moving revenue from the companies to players' pockets or unlicensed alternatives. That is the core of [regulatory risk](/kurser/rk-06-regulatorisk-risk) and [regulatory catalysts](/kurser/v18-regulatoriska): a rule change hits like a quarterly report — but shows in none.

The regulatory map is also the sector's growth engine. Mature markets like Sweden grow a few percent a year — Q1 2026: 6.7 billion kronor (+0.8), Q2: 6.9 (+2.8) — while jurisdictions regulating gambling for the first time open entirely new revenue bases. So you read the sector's growth: the level of mature home markets against the opening of new markets.

## The margins — Evolution as a worked example

The universe's raw data (2026-09-15) shows why B2B suppliers carry the sector's most admired numbers. Evolution reports a gross margin of 100 percent — a source convention: revenue is net of gambling-related fees, without separate cost of goods sold — but further down the income statement the economics count: operating margin 57.8 percent, net margin 51.8 percent, return on invested capital 31.2 percent and debt to equity 0.02. As a worked example: of every 100 euros of revenue, roughly 58 euros become operating income. A B2C operator with the same player volume has far lower margins — fees, marketing and tax take their shares first — which is why operator analysis starts in the player's economics (acquisition cost against lifetime value), supplier analysis in platform scalability. The craft of profitability — [ROE](/blogg/hur-raknar-man-roe) and comparing differently leveraged companies — goes deeper in [ROE analysis](/blogg/v09-roe-analys).

## Growth — mature at home, opening globally

The universe series for Evolution (reporting currency euro): revenue 1,457 → 1,799 → 2,063 → 2,067 million euros for fiscal 2022–2025. Read it as two chapters: strong expansion, then a plateau — the last twelve months show −2.2 percent, while consensus for next year sits at +11.4 percent. So you use the numbers together: P/E 15.15 against forecast growth of 11.4 percent gives PEG = 15.15 ÷ 11.4 ≈ 1.33, and forward P/E 13.60 sits below trailing — the market prices a return to growth, but the calculation rests on a forecast, exactly as [the PEG multiple's weaknesses](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026) warns. The tool for separating trend from pause is [revenue stability analysis](/blogg/v12-intaktsstabilitet-analys): how evenly revenue grew across the period, not just peak to peak. One more detail: Evolution reports in euros but lists in kronor on Nasdaq Stockholm — currency movement sits between operations and your result, a practical example of [currency risk](/kurser/rk-07-valutarisk).

## The mandatory offer — regulation's sharpest edge

The summer of 2026 showed the sector's other regulatory side — corporate control, not game rules. On 24 July 2026 Candle Lake Limited acquired shares taking its holding to 30.02 percent of Evolution, passing the Swedish mandatory offer threshold of 30 percent and forcing a mandatory cash offer. The offer, made 13 August at 695 kronor per share — about 132 billion kronor for the company — sat 5.7 percent below the previous close, and Evolution's board spoke against it and recommended shareholders to decline: the company's own position, showing the process from within. The market's answer is the guide's clearest example: in the universe's raw data (2026-09-15) the share traded at 890.60 kronor — 890.6 ÷ 695 ≈ 1.28, that is 28 percent above the offer price. The price reflects expectations — of a higher bid, a counter-offer or a failed one — not just the offer sum. No conclusion about the outcome can be calculated in advance; this guide refrains from trying. The mechanism to understand is the difference between price and bid, not the guess about the ending.

## How to read the gambling company's report

Five items deserve extra attention. First, the license portfolio: how many jurisdictions the company holds permits in, and which open or close. Second, the revenue share from regulated versus less regulated markets — the sector's single most important risk item, since regulating a large unregulated market can both open and close revenue flows. Third, gambling fees and marketing: how they move relative to revenue — a rising share means harder competition for players. Fourth, B2B customer concentration: how much revenue comes from the largest customers. Fifth, the currency side: reporting currency against listing, and how much revenue is hedged. The reading order in [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) works as framework, and the multiple's comparison within the sector — never against the market at large — is explained in [EV/EBITDA](/blogg/sa-raknar-du-ev-ebitda).

## The summary

- Sort by business model first: operator (B2C — acquisition and player lifetime) against supplier (B2B — platform, scalability, customer concentration). Two economies, one label.
- The license is moat and risk in one: an entry barrier and an 18 percent gambling tax in Sweden, but exposed to rule changes that show in no previous report.
- The Swedish licensed market grows a few percent — Q2 2026: 6.9 billion kronor, +2.8 percent — while global regulation drives the sector's growth.
- The margin hierarchy is real: Evolution's operating margin 57.8 percent in universe data against lower B2C margins; always read the gross margin definition (the net convention gives 100 percent).
- The mandatory offer at 30 percent is part of the sector's regulation: the offer of 695 kronor against the listing of 890.60 — the price reflects expectations, not just the offer sum.
